journeys.rationale: Declaring a new pinning exception removes L7 enforcement for that host, so the review flow must flag it as a change that weakens the egress firewall — the user must not be able to promote it without seeing that.

steps.intent: create a sandbox named pin18 from a project folder whose manifest declares the firewall on with a vendor host allowed normally, and apply that manifest
steps.expect: the sandbox's policy has the vendor host allowed and inspected

steps.intent: edit the manifest so that vendor host's port now carries the certificate-pinning exception, and review the drift
steps.expect: the review marks this change as one that weakens the egress firewall, not as an ordinary settings change

journeys.rationale: The subtler weakening: removing the one entry that pulled a non-web port into the inspected set silently un-inspects every other host still allowed on that port. The review flow must flag that too, even though no exception is declared anywhere.

steps.intent: create a sandbox named pin19 from a manifest whose firewall is on and where two hosts are allowed on the same non-web port, with one of them asking for that port to be policed at the HTTP layer
steps.expect: the sandbox's policy shows that port as inspected

steps.intent: edit the manifest to drop the entry that asked for the policing while leaving the other host reachable on the same port, and review the drift
steps.expect: the review marks this as a change that weakens the egress firewall, because a port that is still reachable stopped being inspected

journeys.rationale: The counterweight: removing an exception, or writing down an inspection that was already true, must NOT be flagged as weakening — a gate that cries wolf on tightening edits stops being read.

steps.intent: create a sandbox named pin20 from a manifest that declares the firewall on with a vendor host whose port carries the certificate-pinning exception, and apply it
steps.expect: the sandbox's policy carries the exception

steps.intent: edit the manifest to remove that exception (leaving the host allowed on the same port), and review the drift
steps.expect: the change is listed but is NOT flagged as weakening the egress firewall

steps.intent: edit the manifest again so a web port is explicitly declared as policed at the HTTP layer (which it already was), and review the drift
steps.expect: this change is likewise not flagged as weakening

journeys.rationale: The same allow-list can be changed two ways with different review properties: the manifest path is gated and flags weakening, while a command-line grant writes the policy immediately with no review. A user should be able to notice that asymmetry rather than assume every change is gated.

steps.intent: create a sandbox named pin21 with an enforcing policy allowing one host
steps.expect: the sandbox is created

steps.intent: from the command line, grant that sandbox an additional host and port
steps.expect: the grant is applied immediately, with no review step and no weakening prompt or warning to acknowledge

steps.intent: print pin21's effective egress policy
steps.expect: the new grant is already in effect

journeys.rationale: The documented way to change a setting the CLI has no flag for: edit the sandbox's managed policy file and reload it. The exception must take effect on a running sandbox without a restart, and be visible afterwards.

source.ref: `izba policy reload --help` — 'edit it there and reload to change settings this CLI has no flag for, such as an entry's `protocol:`'

steps.intent: start a sandbox named pin22 with an enforcing policy allowing a vendor host, and confirm it is running
steps.expect: the sandbox is running

steps.intent: find where izba keeps that sandbox's managed policy, add the certificate-pinning exception to one of the vendor host's ports there, and make izba pick it up without restarting the sandbox
steps.expect: izba accepts the reload with no error and the sandbox is still running

steps.intent: print pin22's effective egress policy
steps.expect: the exception is now reported against that port on the running sandbox

journeys.rationale: A declaration that only lived in memory would be a trap: an operator who restarts the sandbox must get the same posture back, not a quietly re-inspected (or quietly still-open) port.

steps.intent: create and start a sandbox named pin23 whose policy carries the certificate-pinning exception on one port
steps.expect: the sandbox is running

steps.intent: stop the sandbox and start it again, then print its effective egress policy
steps.expect: the exception is still declared against the same port, unchanged by the restart

journeys.rationale: The functional payoff: from inside an enforcing sandbox, a host with the exception must reach its real upstream with the vendor's own certificate (that is the whole point — a pinning client works), while another allowed host is still intercepted with izba's certificate.

steps.intent: create and start a sandbox named pin24 with the firewall on, allowing two real internet hosts on HTTPS, one of which carries the certificate-pinning exception on its HTTPS port
steps.expect: the sandbox is running with the policy in effect

steps.intent: from inside the sandbox, look at which certificate authority signs the certificate presented for the ordinary allowed host
steps.expect: the ordinary host is presented with izba's own interception certificate

steps.intent: from inside the sandbox, look at which certificate authority signs the certificate presented for the host carrying the exception
steps.expect: that host presents its real upstream certificate, not izba's — a client that pins the vendor's certificate would succeed

journeys.rationale: The dormant case, checked against reality rather than the printed line: a pinning exception on a read-only entry does not actually pass anything through, so the client still sees izba's certificate. If the printed posture and the wire disagree, an operator has been told the wrong thing about their firewall.

steps.intent: create and start a sandbox named pin25 whose firewall is on and where a real internet host is restricted to read-only access while carrying the certificate-pinning exception on its HTTPS port
steps.expect: the sandbox is running with the policy in effect

steps.intent: from inside the sandbox, look at which certificate is presented for that host, and compare it with what izba's own policy output says about the exception
steps.expect: the connection is still intercepted (izba's certificate is presented) and izba's printed posture agrees that the exception is not in effect for this entry

journeys.rationale: A pass-through must be bound to the name izba itself resolved, never to whatever the guest claims. Reaching the same destination by raw IP address (bypassing name resolution) must not get the exception.

steps.intent: create and start a sandbox named pin26 with the firewall on, allowing a real internet host on HTTPS with the certificate-pinning exception declared on that port
steps.expect: the sandbox is running with the policy in effect

steps.intent: from inside the sandbox, confirm the exception works when the host is reached by name
steps.expect: the host is reached and presents its own upstream certificate

steps.intent: from inside the sandbox, try to reach the same destination by its raw IP address instead of by name
steps.expect: the raw-address attempt does not get the exception: it is either refused by the firewall or intercepted, never passed through opaquely

journeys.rationale: The exception is keyed to one host, not to the port: another host allowed on the same port must stay fully inspected. An operator granting one vendor an exception must not silently lose enforcement for everything else on 443.

steps.intent: create and start a sandbox named pin27 with the firewall on, allowing two real internet hosts on HTTPS where only one carries the certificate-pinning exception
steps.expect: the sandbox is running with the policy in effect

steps.intent: from inside the sandbox, reach both hosts over HTTPS and compare which certificate each presents
steps.expect: only the host carrying the exception presents its own upstream certificate; the other is still intercepted by izba, so the port itself did not lose inspection

journeys.rationale: Reachability and inspectability are separate axes and the exception may only ever narrow what reachability already permits: declaring the exception for a host that the allow-list does not otherwise permit must not make that host reachable.

steps.intent: create and start a sandbox named pin28 with the firewall on, where the allow-list's only entry is a host declared solely so it can carry the certificate-pinning exception on its HTTPS port — and a second, entirely unlisted host
steps.expect: the sandbox is running with the policy in effect

steps.intent: from inside the sandbox, try to reach the unlisted host over HTTPS
steps.expect: the unlisted host is blocked by the firewall — declaring an exception elsewhere did not open anything up

journeys.rationale: An operator who opens the desktop app to answer 'is anything bypassing my firewall?' must get an answer there. The Policy tab must show the pinned port distinctly and state what it gives up, in substance matching what the command line says.
